newsitem.title: CHINA: China says to sign U.N. covenant on social rights.
newsitem.headline: China says to sign U.N. covenant on social rights.

text.p: China, a focus of controversy over its human rights record, was ready to sign the U.N. International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights before the end of this year, President Jiang Zemin has said.
Government departments were now studying domestic legislation related to the covenant, Jiang told visiting French Defence Minister Charles Millon in a meeting on Monday.

"We evaluated the International Covenant on Economic, Social, and Cultural Rights and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights repeatedly," the Xinhua news agency quoted Jiang as saying in an overnight report.

China was ready to sign the United Nations covenant on economic, social and cultural rights before the end of the year, he said. He did not comment on China's apparent decision not to sign the covenant on civil and political rights.
The Chinese government has made efforts to ensure its people's rights to subsistence and development, and had raised the level of economic, social, and cultural rights, Jiang said.
Beijing had also continued to improve development of democracy and a legal system to ensure the civil and political rights of China's 1.2 billion people, Jiang said.
"The Chinese people in fact enjoy comprehensive human rights," he was quoted as saying.

Jiang praised Paris for its "wise and far-sighted" decision not to co-sponsor a United Nations resolution critical of Beijing's human rights record, hinting that such a move would boost French business with China.
During Chirac's visit, China and France would release a joint statement on their common views on major international issues and common aspirations for expanding ties, he said.

French determination to develop the Sino-French partnership would have an "important and positive" influence on ties, Jiang said, adding that he expected political and economic results from a visit by French President Jacques Chirac next month.

Referring to the proposed motion in the United Nations to censure China over human rights, Jiang said he hoped France would play a role in persuading more Western countries to avoid confrontation in favour of dialogue.
Denmark vowed on Monday to press ahead with the U.N. resolution criticising China's human rights record, defying Beijing's warning that the move would severely damage ties.

Assured of the backing of the United States and most European Union states, with the notable exceptions of France and Germany, Danish Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen said his country would present the resolution this week at the U.N. Human Rights Commission in Geneva.

Previous attempts to condemn China on human rights in a U.N. resolution following Beijing's bloody 1989 crackdown on pro-democracy protesters have failed. China has rallied enough support each year to block the move.
China's Jiang said differing views on human rights were normal and inevitable among different countries with different social systems, cultural traditions and historical backgrounds.
"There is no wonder that there are disputes, but what is more important is the way these disputes are resolved," he was quoted as saying.

In a briefing on China's human rights on Monday, Chinese experts said development of democracy in China would be a gradual process and pro-democracy activists serving jail terms were common criminals convicted by due legal process.
